scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for someone to want their girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks. From what I understand, the girlfriend has a really great job with a lot of flexibility, good benefits, and she seems to be pretty happy with it. But the person feels like she's forgetting that not everyone has such a great job and that her constant talking about her work perks is coming off as braggy. They had an argument about it, and now they're wondering if they were being unreasonable or if they were justified in their feelings. First, I think it's important to consider both sides of the situation. On one hand, the girlfriend has worked hard to get where she is, and she's entitled to be proud of her achievements. It's natural for people to want to share positive things about their lives, especially with their partner. On the other hand, the person feels like she's being oblivious to the fact that not everyone has such a great job, and that her constant talking about her perks is making them uncomfortable. Maybe the issue is not so much that she's bragging, but rather that she's not considering how her words might affect others. It's possible that she doesn't realize that her lifestyle is not the norm, and that talking about it so much could make others feel inadequate or jealous. However, it's also possible that the person is projecting their own insecurities or frustrations onto her, which could be making the situation worse. I think communication is key here. Instead of accusing her of being braggy, the person could try to express their feelings in a more constructive way. For example, they could say something like, "I feel like we're always talking about your job, and it makes me feel like my own struggles aren't being acknowledged." This way, they're expressing their feelings without attacking her, which might make her more receptive to their concerns. It's also important to consider the context in which these conversations are happening. If they're among friends who are aware of her job situation, it might not be as big of a deal. But if they're around people who don't have similar opportunities, it could be more sensitive. The girlfriend might not realize that her comments are making others feel bad, especially if she's not intentionally trying to boast. Another angle to consider is the dynamic of the relationship. If the person is feeling insecure or jealous, it might be helpful for them to reflect on why they're feeling that way. Are there underlying issues that need to be addressed? Maybe they feel like they're not achieving as much as their partner, or perhaps they're envious of her success. Addressing these feelings individually or with the help of a therapist could be beneficial. In terms of whether the person was "AITA" (Ask If It's Too Much), I think it's a bit of a gray area. It's understandable that they feel frustrated if they feel like their partner is not considering their feelings or the feelings of others. However, the way they expressed their frustration might have come across as accusatory or dismissive, which could have made the situation worse. It might have been more effective to approach the conversation with empathy and understanding, rather than making her feel like she's doing something wrong. Overall, I think the situation highlights the importance of open and honest communication in relationships. Both partners need to feel heard and understood, and it's important to approach sensitive topics with kindness and respect. If the person can express their feelings in a constructive way, and the girlfriend can be more mindful of how her words might affect others, they can work together to improve their relationship.
